# Naḷapānajātaka (Ja 20)

**ID:** Ja 20
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Naḷapānajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Drinking With Straws

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Naḷapānajātaka* (Ja 20) is the twentieth story in the Pali *Jātaka* collection, standing as the tenth and concluding discourse of the *Sīlavagga* [Fausböll 1877]. The framing narrative is set in Kosala, where the Buddha was residing at the Ketakavana grove near the village pool of Naḷakapāna [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. When monks discovered that cane reeds collected from the pool by novices to serve as needle-cases were hollow throughout from top to bottom, they questioned the Buddha regarding this anomaly [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a wise monkey-king leading a troop of eighty thousand monkeys [Fiordalis 2011; Fausböll 1877]. Finding the pool inhabited by a malevolent water demon (*dakarakkhasa*, later identified with Devadatta), the monkey-king safeguarded his troop by calling to mind the perfections (*pāramī*), uttering an act of truth, and blowing through a cane reed [Fiordalis 2011; Fausböll 1877]. This act miraculously hollowed out all the reeds surrounding the pond, enabling the monkeys to drink safely as though through straws without entering the water [SuttaCentral; Fiordalis 2011]. Within Buddhist miracle traditions, this event is classified as one of the four epoch-long miracles (*kappaṭṭhiya pāṭihāriya*) that endure for an entire age, highlighting how truth utterances demonstrate the Bodhisatta's progression toward Buddhahood [Fiordalis 2011].

According to SuttaCentral, a full parallel to the narrative is preserved in the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu* under the title *The Jātaka of the Monkey (1)* (San Lo Mvu 68) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identified no significant Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language matches with a score of 10 or higher [DharmaNexus].
